nameStory: The 'nipple' in Nipple Lichen comes from its distinctive rounded, dome-like structures that dot the lichen's surface like tiny bumps. These nipple-shaped projections are actually the lichen's reproductive structures, called apothecia, which contain spores for reproduction.
description: Nipple Lichen is a small, crusty lichen that forms patches on decaying wood and bark. It creates thin, grayish-white to pale green crusts that are peppered with small, rounded bumps that give it its distinctive appearance. Individual patches typically grow 1-3 inches across, though multiple colonies can merge to cover larger areas of suitable substrate.

idTips.label: Reproductive Structures
idTips.description: Small, rounded, nipple-like bumps (apothecia) dot the surface, feeling firm and slightly raised when you run your finger gently across them

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Forms a thin, crusty coating (crustose) that's tightly attached to the surface and cannot be peeled off without damaging it

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Pale grayish-white to light greenish-gray when dry, becoming more vibrant green when wet from rain or dew

idTips.label: Substrate
idTips.description: Almost exclusively found on decaying wood, particularly weathered logs, old stumps, and the dead portions of tree bark

idTips.label: Surface Texture
idTips.description: Feels slightly rough and granular to the touch, like fine sandpaper, with a somewhat powdery appearance in dry conditions

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Individual patches range from coin-sized to palm-sized, with the characteristic bumps being quite small, about 1-2mm across

habitat: Look for Nipple Lichen in moist, shaded woodlands throughout New England, particularly in areas with plenty of decaying wood. It thrives on old logs, stumps, and dead branches in both coniferous and mixed forests, preferring spots that stay humid but aren't constantly waterlogged. You'll often find it alongside mosses and other wood-dwelling lichens in the forest understory.

seasonality.spring: The lichen appears brighter green as spring moisture activates growth, and the nipple-like reproductive structures may be most prominent as spore production increases.
seasonality.summer: During dry summer periods, the lichen fades to pale gray-white and may look dusty or powdery, with reproductive bumps still clearly visible.
seasonality.fall: Fall rains rejuvenate the lichen's green coloration, and it becomes more noticeable as deciduous leaves drop and expose more of its woody substrate.
seasonality.winter: Snow and ice may partially obscure the lichen, but it remains visible year-round, appearing grayish and dormant until moisture returns.

funFact: Despite being called Nipple Lichen for its bumpy appearance, those 'nipples' are actually tiny spore-shooting cannons that can explosively release thousands of reproductive spores when conditions are just right!
confusionNotes: Nipple Lichen is most easily confused with other crusty lichens on wood, but the distinctive rounded bumps are the key differentiator. Remember: 'nipples on wood' - if you see those characteristic dome-shaped projections on decaying timber, you've likely found your target.
contextualKnowledge: The scientific name Pycnothelia comes from Greek words meaning 'thick nipple,' directly referencing the prominent rounded reproductive structures that make this lichen so distinctive and relatively easy to identify among the often-confusing world of crusty lichens.
compareHints: Since Nipple Lichen is the only species in its genus Pycnothelia found in New England, compare it with other crusty wood-dwelling lichens in the Cladoniaceae family. Unlike the cup-shaped or branching forms of Cladonia species that grow nearby, Nipple Lichen maintains its flat, crusty growth with distinctively rounded bumps rather than hollow cups or vertical branches.
